sm: The episode opens with the claim that physicians traditionally acted for the patient's health and refused to harm it, while today's provider of services model asks them to do things that seem contrary to health, such as abortion, assisted suicide and euthanasia. Speakers argue that when human life begins is settled by science at fertilization, citing a survey of several thousand scientists in which ninety six percent agreed, and that the real dispute is when our responsibility for life begins. They say dehumanizing language, like calling a wanted child a baby but an unwanted one a clump of cells or products of conception, makes setting people aside easier. They point to the Hippocratic Oath's promise not to give an abortive remedy and criticize Peter Singer's idea of a human non-person. The part ends by introducing Jack Kevorkian, who helped more than one hundred thirty terminally ill patients die.

This part turns to physician-assisted suicide, which speakers describe as legal in a handful of states, including California, where a doctor writes a prescription for a deadly drug that the patient takes. A palliative medicine physician says patients now wonder about hastening death, and that supporters argue it treats unbearable suffering and respects autonomy. Critics say a six month prognosis limit invites the question of why others who suffer longer are excluded, and warn that insurers might subtly pressure vulnerable patients because home care is costly. They note that in Canada eligibility widened from a six month prognosis to foreseeable death, then to mental illness, with court fights over children, and that the top reason patients give is autonomy and control. They conclude that once it is legal, every eligible person must ask why not me, and that eliminating suffering must not mean eliminating the sufferer.
